summary:
EarthPulse is an interactive Earth observation platform designed to visualize and analyze changes in Earth's surface using NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) satellite data. The project leverages multi-temporal SAR observations to identify, compare, and highlight surface changes over a selected Area of Interest (AOI), making complex radar data easier to understand through intuitive visualizations.

By processing NISAR Level-2 Geocoded (GCOV) data across multiple observation dates, EarthPulse aims to reveal environmental changes that may not be easily visible through conventional optical satellite imagery. The platform transforms complex scientific datasets into accessible visual insights, helping users explore patterns of surface change and better understand environmental dynamics.

EarthPulse addresses the challenge of making advanced Earth observation data more accessible, interpretable, and useful. It demonstrates how satellite radar technology can support environmental monitoring, scientific exploration, and evidence-based decision-making.
details: EarthPulse is an interactive Earth observation and surface-change analysis platform built around NASA-ISRO's NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) mission. It transforms complex satellite radar measurements into understandable visual information, allowing users to explore how Earth's surface changes over time. How It Works EarthPulse uses NISAR Level-2 Geocoded (GCOV) radar observations collected at different times over the same geographical area. Our prepared dataset includes observations from three acquisition cycles: 028, 032, and 033, covering multiple observation periods in 2026. The platform follows a multi-temporal analysis approach: 1. Satellite Data Acquisition: Obtains NISAR radar observations and their associated geospatial metadata. 2. Data Processing: Prepares and organizes radar datasets for comparison, including spatial alignment and valid-data assessment. 3. Temporal Comparison: Compares radar measurements from different observation dates to identify changes in surface characteristics. 4. Change Analysis: Uses radar-derived information to investigate changes that may indicate environmental transformations. 5. Visualization: Presents the analysis through an interactive interface, making complex satellite observations easier to explore and interpret. Benefits and Intended Impact Unlike conventional optical satellite imagery, synthetic aperture radar can collect observations through clouds and independently of sunlight. This makes NISAR particularly valuable for monitoring areas where optical observations may be limited. EarthPulse aims to make advanced satellite observations more accessible to students, researchers, environmental organizations, and decision-makers. Its intended applications include monitoring environmental changes, investigating wetland and coastal dynamics, supporting scientific research, and improving awareness of changes occurring across Earth's surface. Technology and Development Tools Our development workflow uses: - NASA-ISRO NISAR: Primary source of satellite radar observations. - NISAR Level-2 GCOV: Geocoded radar datasets for multi-temporal analysis. - Google Antigravity: Primary development environment for building the application. - Google Gemini 3.8 Flash: AI-assisted development and implementation. - OpenCode: Supporting data validation, technical verification, and development tasks. - Machine Learning: Planned integration for extracting meaningful patterns and supporting surface-change analysis. Creativity and Innovation The central innovation of EarthPulse is turning complex radar measurements into an understandable, time-based exploration of Earth's changing surface. Instead of treating satellite observations as isolated images, EarthPulse approaches them as a sequence of scientific measurements that can be compared across time. We also considered data quality, geographical consistency, observation availability, temporal comparability, and scientific reliability when preparing the datasets. Our goal is not simply to visualize satellite data, but to help people understand what those measurements can reveal about our changing planet.
